en: Oṃ, the consecration of Bhadrakālī.
(Front page is blank) (f.1a, line 1)
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme installation of Cāmuṇḍā,
whether in a village or a city, on a mountain peak or in forests.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, gandharvas, mṛgas, and rākṣasas—
whatever terrible fear exists in that village, it will undoubtedly perish.
It brings about the entry [of the deity], the destruction of great boils,
the eradication of non-ash and stones, and the destruction of great defects.
Furthermore, the installation of Cāmuṇḍā, especially in villages and other such places,
brings about the arrival of the nine crores of great Śaktis and the gods themselves.
In the midst of that is Cāmuṇḍā, the great power, the foremost leader;
she who effects the establishment of the village, and whatever auspicious installation of the Lord of Passion (Rāgeśa) there may be.
During the period of the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, one should invoke and worship the Goddess.
Having first gathered the clay according to the eighteenfold method, one should then construct the sacrificial hall together with [the teacher] according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should construct fire-pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one, two, three, or four cubits in length, width, and depth as required, resembling the surface of a mirror,
specifically arranged starting from the east.
Specifically, the lotus-pool extends from the east to the north.
In the northeast, one should fashion the goddess’s sacrificial pit in the shape of a womb;
having smeared it with cow dung, perform the rite of circumambulation with fire.

Then the Guru, having performed the two daily rites (*nityāhnika*) together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipāḥ*), proceeds to the sacrificial hall (*makha-ālaya*). Seated upon a beautiful seat and facing north, he performs three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having meditated upon Bhadrakālī and contemplated her permission, he performs the worship of Vighneśvara first, recites the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and the declaration of auspiciousness (*puṇyāha*), and sprinkles [the area] with water. Between Indra and Agni, he worships Śiva-Sūrya as in the daily ritual, and having dismissed him, he sips water for purification (*ācamana*).

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having consecrated the general offering (sāmānyārghya), one should take the arghya vessel in one's own hand, stand outside the pavilion, sprinkle the eastern gate with the Astra-mantra, and shield it with the Kavaca-mantra. In the middle of the archway (toraṇa), [one should worship]:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Peaceful Archway (śāntitoraṇa); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Peaceful Archway.
[The deity is] dressed in blue garments and blue unguents, possessing two arms joined in the añjali gesture.
One should indeed meditate upon the dark-complexioned Karālavadana, who possesses peaceful gateways.

Oṃ hāṃ (fourth line), obeisance to Śāntitoraṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhadra, the lord of Śāntitoraṇa. On the two arch-branches [are] the two [deities], dark-complexioned, two-eyed, one-faced, and four-armed.
Salutation to the one holding a ghaṇṭī and a rosary, and making the añjali gesture of the Ṛgveda.

(5th line) Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Ṛgveda. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kṛta Yuga. Upon the trident: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Salutation to Narmadā. (6th line)
On the northern banner of the door: *namaḥ* to Praśānta. On the southern banner of the door: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Śiśira. On the upper lintel (*udumbara*):
*oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Gaṇapati; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Sarasvatī;
*oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Mahālakṣmī. On the southern and northern door-frames: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Nandin; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Ādiśakti; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Mahākāla; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Padaniśakti.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. (8th line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dehinīśakti. At the lower part of the doorpost: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the weapon-guardian of the door. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Durgā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Ka-group. On the banner situated above the door: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Budha. Having worshipped these [deities] with perfumes and other offerings, one offers the *arghya* at the southeast banner (the *āgneya-dhvaja*) with: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agni; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Svāhādevī. Having sprinkled the southern door with the *astra-mantra* and concealed it with the *kavaca-mantra*, [one worships] in the middle of the archway (*toraṇa*) with: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of the Bhūti-archway;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of the Bhūti-archway.
Having two arms and two eyes, adorned with black ornaments,
he is described as having a gateway of spirits, a neck like a pillar, and a large belly.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhūtitoraṇa. (Third line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vijaya, the lord of Bhūtitoraṇa. On the two branches of the archway [one should visualize him] red in color, with two eyes, and wearing a white sacred thread.
One should visualize the Yajurveda as having become a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) and a handful of water (*añjali*).

(4th line) *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Yajurveda. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Tretā Age. On the trident: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Manonmanī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Sarasvatī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Sindhu. On the eastern banner of the door: (5th line) *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Parjanya. Salutation to the western banner of the door: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Aśoka. On the upper *udumbara* beam: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Gaṇapati. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Sarasvatī. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. (6th line)

On the eastern and western door-posts: *oṃ hāṃ hlādini-śaktyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vināyakāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vallabhāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kālakaṇṭhyai namaḥ*. At the lower threshold: *oṃ hāṃ astrāyā-dvārapālakāya namaḥ*. (7th line) *oṃ hāṃ cavargāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *ṭa*-group of consonants. To the banner situated above the door: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bṛhaspati; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhārgava. To the banner in the *Nairṛta* corner: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nairṛti; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dehini-Śakti. (8th line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (*Vāstvādhipati*). Having worshipped [these], one should sprinkle the western door-arch with the *astra-mantra* and envelop it with the *kavaca-mantra*.

In the middle of the archway: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Bala-archway; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Bala-archway.* I meditate upon the Bala-archway, which is red in color, two-eyed, with a serpent as its sacred thread, and joined with palms pressed together in reverence.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the strong archway (balatoraṇa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vajra, the lord of the strong archway. To him who is white in color, two-eyed, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and joined with the staff of the Brahmā-missile and the Sāmaveda—to him I bow.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sāmaveda. (3rd line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Dvāpara Yuga. On the trident: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Godāvarī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Umā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kāverī. On the southern banner: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhūtasañjīvana. On the northern banner (4th line): Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Amṛtasañjīvana. On the upper crossbeam: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the southern and northern branches: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha. (5th line)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhadrā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śacīsuta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vaśiṇī. At the lower *dumbara* tree: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Astra, the protector of the door. To the north: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *tavarga*. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *pavarga*. On the banner situated above the door: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aṅgāra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.

Having thus worshipped, and having sprinkled the northern door with the Astra-mantra, and having shielded it with the Kavaca-mantra, [one should worship] in the middle of the archway: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Archway of Health (Ārogyatoraṇa). "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form (mūrti) of the Archway of Health.
[It is] two-armed, two-eyed, and has long hair hanging down on both sides.
One should worship the Health Archway (Ārogyatoraṇa), whose face is formidable with fangs.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Health Archway. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nīlalohita, the lord of the Health Archway.
On the two branches of the archway, one should worship Kṛṣṇa, who has four arms and holds a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary.
Alternatively, one should worship him holding his hands together in the añjali gesture.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Atharvaveda. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kali Yuga. On the trident: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śoṇabhadra; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhāgīrathī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aṅgabhadrā. On the western door-banner: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dhanada. On the eastern banner: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrīprada. On the upper *udumbara* beam: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. On the western and eastern branches: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Goddess.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rūpiṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the power Bhātirī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera.

At the lower *dumbara* [beam], Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the weapon-gatekeeper (*astradvārapāla*). (4th line) Obeisance to the *ya*-group. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *śa*-group. On the banner situated above the door, Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāhu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ketu. On the banner in the northeast corner, Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. (5th line)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śakti Harṣaṇī.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Gurus beginning with Sadāśiva. Having worshipped these with all the ritual offerings (upacāras), such as invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, [one proceeds as follows]:

at the northern *vardhanī* from the eastern doors, [one offers] "Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the door-seat of the Śāntikalā" (oṃ haiṃ śāntikalā dvārāsanāya namaḥ); and "Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the door-form of the Śāntikalā" (oṃ haiṃ śāntikalā-dvāramūrtaye namaḥ).
Four-faced, four-armed, black in color, and possessed of great strength;
holding a banner, a rosary, and a lotus, she is peaceful and has a serpent as her sacred thread.
(7th line) Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Śāntikalā. To the north of that, on the seat of Sāmambikā: Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Sāmambikā; Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Sāmambikā.
One should meditate upon Ambikā, who has four arms and two eyes, holding a rosary and a water-pot, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness.
(8th line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ambikā. Jyaḥ, obeisance to the seat of Gaṇāmbikā on the southern threshold of the door.
One should meditate upon Gaṇāmbikā, who has four arms and three eyes, who holds a noose and a goad, who is auspicious, and who displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇāmbikā. Jyaḥ: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the door of the Vidyā-kalā at the eastern corner of the southern gate.
Red in color, with matted hair and a crescent moon, three-faced and four-armed, holding a spear, a rosary, and a lotus, she resembles the blazing fire of knowledge.
(2nd line) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vidyākalā. To the east of that, in the *vardhanī*, Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgāsana.

[One should meditate upon] Gaṅgā, who has three eyes, is white in complexion, holds a deer and an axe, is radiant, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is seated upon a crocodile.
(3rd line) *Oṃ hāṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ* [at the western side of the doorway]; *Oṃ hāṃ gaurīyai namaḥ*.

For the accomplishment of all aims, one should meditate upon the dark-complexioned Gaurī with four arms, holding a lotus and a water-lily, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to Gaurī (fourth line).
On the southern threshold of the western door: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one whose seat is the door of the Nivṛtti-kalā.
She has the luster of molten gold and is adorned with four faces and the moon.
Holding a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a rosary, and a lotus, Nivṛtti bestows all accomplishments.
(5th line) *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the digit of cessation (*nivṛttikalā*). JYA. To its south, in Vardhaṇī: *Oṃ sāṃ*, salutation to Umāsana.
Umā herself is blue in color, auspicious, and holds a conch and a discus.
[One should worship] her who is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who creates the worlds and houses.
Oṃ Sām, obeisance to Umā. Jya. At the northern door-post: Oṃ Dhām, obeisance to Īśvaryāsanā.
She has four arms and two eyes, and is adorned with various ornaments.
Adorned with an eye, a bow, and a lotus, and endowed with the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons.
Oṃ, salutation to Sāmīśvarī. *Jya*. At the western *vardhanī* of the northern gate: Oṃ Hvīṃ, salutation to the seat of the door of the *Pratiṣṭhā-kalā*.
She resembles pure crystal, has one face and four arms;
she holds a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, and is adorned with the nature of *Pratiṣṭhā*.
Oṃ hvīṃ, obeisance to the digit of Installation (Pratiṣṭhā-kalā). Jya. Then, on the western *vardhanī* [vessel]: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Manonmanī.
[One should visualize] the Goddess who has three eyes, is red in color, holds two lotuses in her hands, grants the boons of fearlessness and prosperity, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. On the banner situated above the intermediate space: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śāntyatītakalāsana.
She is white in color, has two eyes, and is adorned with a basket-shaped crown (karaṇḍa-makuṭa);
she holds a lotus and a blue water-lily in her hands, and is endowed with the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dhārikā. Above the banner in the middle of the sky: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śāntyatītakalāsana.
Resembling pure crystal, five-faced, and four-armed;
holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus; she bestows the boon of Śāntyatīta.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śāntyatīta-kalā. Having worshipped thus, one should propitiate the gatekeepers at the western door as is done regularly, as follows: (4th line) having sprinkled the door with the Astra-mantra; above the door, on the right, left, and center: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Narmadā; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. On the right side of the door: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā. (5th line)

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Yoginī. On the left side: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Yamunā; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ḍākinī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sindhu; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Godāvarī. (Sixth line) In the middle of the lower door-posts: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kāverī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi; in front, obeisance to Vṛṣabha. Having worshipped thus and offered water for the feet and other offerings, [one should employ] the Mūla-weapon and the Pāśupata-weapon. (Seventh line)

Having dispelled the obstacles situated in the divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms with the weapon-mantra, and having joined [the deities] together, [one should worship them] at the western door, in the lower part of the *udumbara* post, and in the center. [One should visualize the deity] with four faces and four arms, possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire, holding in the right and left hands, respectively, a spear (*śakti*), a trident (*śūla*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*vara*).

Having worshipped with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the weapon, the guardian of the door," and leaning slightly against the left door-post, he enters within with his right foot leading. Having circumambulated the sacrificial hall in the clockwise direction and standing in the southwest (Nairṛta), if the pavilion is covered with grass and the like, [he should worship]: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the earth element" for the grass; "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the water element" for the straw; and "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the fire element" for the binding cords.

In the rafters: *oṃ hāṃ vāyutattvāya namaḥ*. In the beams: *oṃ hāṃ ākāśatattvāya namaḥ*. On the pinnacle: *śivāya namaḥ*. In the canopies: *vajrāya namaḥ*. In the ripples: *oṃ hāṃ jāhnavyai namaḥ*. In the garland of *darbha* grass: *oṃ hāṃ vasukyai namaḥ*. In the courtyard: *oṃ hāṃ mugarāya namaḥ*. In the directions: *oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*. Around the secondary altar, starting from the east and ending with the north-east: on the mirror held by Urvaśī, *darpaṇādhipataye sūryāya namaḥ*.

Salutation to Uṣādevī; salutation to Menakā holding a full water-pot, to Jaleśvara, the lord of the full water-pot; salutation to Jāhnavī; salutation to Rambhā holding a pair of swans, to Īśvara, the lord of the pair of swans; salutation to Umā; salutation to Tilottamā holding a pair of chowries, to Mātariśvan, the lord of the pair of chowries; salutation to Kālī; salutation to Sumukhī holding the Śrīvatsa mark, to Mahālakṣmī, the lord of the Śrīvatsa.

"Salutation to Bhūdevī; salutation to Sundaridhṛtasvastika, the Lord of the Svastika; salutation to Raudrī; salutation to Svāhādevī; salutation to Kāmukidhṛtaśaṅkha, the pure Lord of the Śaṅkha. (7th line) Having thus worshipped with "Salutation to Śaśidevī; salutation to Kāmavardhanidhṛtadīpa, the fiery-tongued Lord of the Dīpa; salutation to Svadhādevī," one should then visualize the pavilion as pervading up to the end of the Śakti-tattva. Afterwards, on the southern side of the altar, upon a tortoise-seat (*kūrmasana*), [one should proceed]. (8th line)

Having sat down facing north upon a tiger skin and other such seats, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the inner sacrifice (*antaryajana*), the oblation (*havana*), and the meditation on the *śivahasta*. Then, having taken [the materials] over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited seven times and tied them to one's right hip, one should duly prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Next, having consecrated with the *astra-mantra* seven times each the parched grain (*lāja*), sandalwood, white mustard, ashes, flowers, *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and pure parched grain used as scattered offerings (*vikirān*), and having collected them in a pure vessel, one should place the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) upon it.

Having cast [the vessel] down, empowered it seven times with the *pāśupatāstra* mantra, purified it through the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and empowered it again with the *saṃhitā* mantra; then, standing in the southwest (*naiṛta*), having consecrated it with the fourfold purificatory rites beginning with inspection—namely: inspection with the root mantra (*mūla*); sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the *astra* mantra; striking (*tāḍana*) with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the *kavaca* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; and [finally] with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having consecrated the twelve [items]— digging, scattering, filling, leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, smearing, making adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*), and the four [edges] ending with the *dhānta*— and having sprinkled them with the water of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should take up the sword of wisdom (*jñānakhaḍga*) and scatter the *vikira* offerings, which take the form of various weapons, for the purpose of pacifying obstructing spirits in the intermediate space.

With a bundle of *kuśa* grass, he should establish Śiva upon the northeast corner of the altar using the Śiva-Gāyatrī for the seat of Vardhanī; in the southwest, [he should offer] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Brahmā" (6th line),
and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Brahmā"— [visualizing him as] seated upon a swan, pot-bellied, fair-complexioned, with a beard and four faces.
Holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot in his right and left hands respectively.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (Vāstvādhipati). To the south of Vāyu, on the *vardhanī* vessel: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī, the consort (Snāyā). The wise one, having meditated upon her who faces the door—dark-hued and showering floods of flowers and jewels—and remembering her as being in the form of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), should worship her with oblations.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. Having meditated upon that [goddess] in the form of the Śakti-maṇḍala, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated in the northeast. In its center, having installed Śiva and the Pāśupatāstra along with the Vardhanī vessel, and having worshipped them with the lotuses of Ananta, Adharma, Jñāna, and Vairāgya, [one should proceed] at the seat of Śiva.

Having worshipped the jar-form with the *mūrtijapa* mantra, and having worshipped therein the Lord Śiva together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), free from the obstruction of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-rodha*), one should [place] the seat in the form of the *mūrti* upon the *vardhanī* vessel— which is a mere fist in size, facing west, and mounted upon a lion-throne— to the south of that.

Having invoked the Pāśupata weapon, having made it whole (*sakalīkṛtya*), and having sprinkled it, then in the directions starting from the east, [one should worship] in the northern *vardhanī* of the sun: *oṃ hāṃ yoginyai namaḥ* | *jyā* | in the south: *oṃ hāṃ siddhayoginyāsnāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ divyayoginimūrttaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ divyayoginyai namaḥ* | *jyā* | (third line) | *jyā* |

In the south-east: *namaḥ* to the seat of Yoginī; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the form of Yoginī; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to Yoginī. [Jyā] In the south: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the seat of Siddhayoginī; *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the seat of Siddhayoginī; *namaḥ* to the form of Siddhayoginī;

*namaḥ* to Siddhayoginī. (4th line) In the south-west: *namaḥ* to the seat of Gaṇeśvarī; *namaḥ* to the form of Gaṇeśvarī; *namaḥ* to Gaṇeśvarī. In the west: *oṃ hāṃ*, *namaḥ* to the seat of Pretāśinī; *namaḥ* to the form of Pretāśinī. (5th line)

*Oṃ namo pretāśinyai namaḥ* | *Jya* | To the seat of Ḍākinī in the northwest, obeisance; to the form of Ḍākinī, obeisance; to Ḍākinī, obeisance | *Jya* | To the seat of Kālī in the north, obeisance; to the form of Kālī, obeisance; to Kālī, obeisance | *Jya* | (6th line) To the seat of Kālarātri in the northeast, obeisance; to the form of Kālarātri, obeisance; to Kālarātri, obeisance | *Jya* | To the south of the northeast, to the seat of Niśācarī, obeisance; to the form of Niśācarī, obeisance; to Niśācarī, obeisance | (7th line)

At the north-western [corner], one should worship the eighteen weapons beginning with: *oṃ hāṃ ḍakkāryāsanāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ḍakkarimūrttaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ḍakkāryai namaḥ*. Having worshipped these with all the services (*upacāras*), such as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, [one should worship] the sword with *oṃ hāṃ khaḍgāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* and the thunderbolt (*vajra*) with *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
O you, O Coṭita! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction, remain alert until the conclusion of the sacrifice; this is my command for you at this time.

In this sequence, one should cause all the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) to hear the command of Kālī. Thereafter, taking the *vardhanī* vessel, and reciting "Oṃ namaḥ sarvātmakāya," one should remember Bhṛgu while pouring the water from its stream into the auspicious jar (*śivakumbha*) with the water-mantra. Having rotated [the vessel] starting from Īśāna and ending at Īśāna, one should again place the jar in its original position.

Then, having established the rear half [of the seat] and worshipped the firm seat (*sthirāsana*), one should perform the meditation on the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*)—extending up to the Power (*śakti*) with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ māyāśaktaye namaḥ*—and likewise on the form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*). Having performed the placement of the limbs (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*), the head (*muṇḍabhaṅgi*), the faces (*vaktrabhaṅgi*), and the digits (*kalābhaṅgi*), as well as the placement of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) and the eyes (*netranyāsa*), one should invoke the clouds and other elements with the root mantra. Having announced "Welcome" and offered the guest-water of welcome (*svāgatārghya*), one should perform the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādyanyāsa*) and the protective veiling (*rakṣāvakuṇṭhana*).

Having displayed the *amṛta-mudrā* and bound the *pañcamukhī-mudrā*, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two feet with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*; water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the five faces beginning with Īśāna with the mantra ending in *svadhā*; and likewise, the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) into the five heads with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. One should present *dūrvā* grass, flowers, parched grain, and so forth. While ringing the bell with the left hand, having offered the water for sipping and the *arghya*, [one performs] the anointing, rubbing with unguents, bathing, and so on.

Having visualized the components of the ritual bath (*snapanāṅga*) and having consecrated [the deity] with special *arghya* water, one should mentally offer with devotion sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, scented unbroken rice (*akṣata*), *dūrvā* grass, a golden loincloth, a girdle, a sacred thread (*upavīta*), earrings, ornaments, and variegated garments.

Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and having adorned [the deity] with the *iṇḍa* and other implements, as well as garlands of flowers, while ringing the bell, one should display the *manoratha-mudrā*. Then, having worshipped the Brahma-aṅgas at their respective places of dissolution, [one worships] the *bhogāṅga* in the location of the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).

Having worshipped with the Brahmāṇḍa offering, and having displayed the *namaskāra-mudrā* while reciting *padma*, *triśūla*, and *makara*, one should establish oneness [with the deity] by means of the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Having worshipped Śiva with the root mantra, one should worship the Weapon (*astra*) in the *vardhanī* vessel with: *oṃ hāṃ astrāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; astramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
[One should meditate upon it as] resembling ten million suns and possessing the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Three-eyed, with a serpent as his sacred thread, four-faced, and four-armed.
With the tips of his teeth blazing, with his eyebrows, beard, and topknot aflame, holding a spear,
a mallet, a trident, and a sword in his hands, and marked with upward lines.

Having thus performed the burning away (*dahana*), having invoked [the deity] with *oṃ ślīṃ paṃ śūṃ hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, and having unified [the deity] with the heart and other limbs using *oṃ hāṃ* and so forth, one should worship those two, adorned with perfumes and other offerings, with all the ritual services (*upacāra*). Having offered incense and lamps, one should worship Ananta and the others in the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), Nandin and the others in the third enclosure, Indra and the others in the fourth enclosure, and Vajra and the others in the fifth enclosure. Having completed the worship up to the offering of food (*naivedya*), water for drinking, betel, and so forth, ending with the recitation (*japa*), one should say: *oṃ hrīṃ śivaśaktibhyāṃ namaḥ*.
Having touched the *kumbha* with the thumb and the *vardhanī* with the fist,
and having offered praise and approval, saying: "Obeisance to you, Śaṅkara, who possesses the form of a *liṅga* for Umā, whose nature is the *bhaga*."
"You are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this immovable form is yours.
This sword of knowledge is yours; take up your own weapon.

(6th line) Having thus offered the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and having offered it, one should recite [the mantra] one-tenth as many times over the *vardhanī* vessel. (7th line)
"I have offered this sacrifice for you, O sacrificer;
therefore, it must now be protected by you until its completion."
Having thus requested protection and performed the *nirodhārghya* (the oblation for cessation), one should offer the *arghya* with that water while reciting the *anirodha-aghora* mantra.

Then, having placed that vessel there itself in a steady position, one should contemplate the removal of all remaining obstacles on every side by means of the *vardhanī*, the seat, the *vikara*, and the *ūrdhvāstra*. Following that, [one should worship] in the wind-filled jar:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vighnavināyaka; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vighnavināyaka."
Since this sacrifice was commenced by us before the Lord of the Gods for the sake of favoring the sacrificial animals, may it proceed to its conclusion without obstacle in your presence.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vighnavināyaka. Jya.
O Lord, foremost of the Skandas, sovereign of the hosts of Gaṇas, husband of Vallabhā and other consorts,
be gracious so that this Śakti-sacrifice may proceed without obstacles.
Having thus made this request, [one should worship] to the west of Īśāna:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seven gurus beginning with Sadāśiva; [and to] Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and again Ambikā."
One should worship Guha, Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, and the Gurus while recollecting them.
Having thus informed [the deity] and offered the general *arghya* water, one should subsequently draw an eight-petaled lotus on the altar with rice grains, unhusked rice, and sesame seeds.
In its center, having placed the vessel for Bhadrakālī and installed the eight Śaktis around it, one should offer: *oṃ hāṃ māyā-śaktaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ anantāsanāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*.

(5th line) Oṃ hāṃ vāsukyai namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ takṣakāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ kārkoṭakāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ śaṅkhapālāya namaḥ | (6th line) Oṃ hāṃ guḷikāya namaḥ. In the center of that: Oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ. In the [directions] beginning with Agneyī: Oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ.

Oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ (7th line) | Oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ in the directions starting from the east. Oṃ hāṃ adharmāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ ajñānāya namaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ avairāgyāya namaḥ (8th line) | [Oṃ hāṃ] anaiśvaryāya namaḥ in the south, north, and middle. Oṃ hāṃ rājasāya namaḥ.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tāmasa; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sāttvika—in the center. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lion Throne. In the [directions] beginning with the southeast: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Kṛta Age; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Tretā Age; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Dvāpara Age; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Kali Age.

In the directions beginning with the east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Unmanifest; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Niyati; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālā. In the center of that: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Keśava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Lower Cover. In the third line.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the upper covering. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the yoga seat. Upon that: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the sprout. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the shoot. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the stalk. (4th line) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the petals. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the filaments. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the pericarp. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seeds. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus. (5th line)

On the circumference at the tip of the petals: *oṃ hāṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ sūryamaṇḍalādhipāyai kriyāyai namaḥ*. On the tips of the filaments: *oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalādhipāyai jñānyai namaḥ*. On the circumference at the tip of the pericarp: *oṃ hāṃ vanhimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ vanhimaṇḍalādhipāyai īśānyai namaḥ*.
In the center of the pericarp: *oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalādhipāyai kuṭilāśaktaye namaḥ*;
*oṃ hāṃ vimalāsanāyai namaḥ*. Above that: *oṃ hāṃ raktacāmuṇḍāsanāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ raktacāmuṇḍamūrtyai namaḥ*. Thus [one should contemplate] the form (*mūrti*) in the nature of radiant light.

One should place [the image], which is staff-shaped and has undivided limbs, upon the vessel-cover; having performed the installation of the twenty-six *kalās*, one should recite: *oṃ hrīṃ raktacāmuṇḍyai namaḥ* on the head;
*oṃ hrīṃ mahācāmuṇḍyai namaḥ* on the mouth; *oṃ hrīṃ medhāyai namaḥ* on the eyes; *oṃ hrīṃ kāḻyai namaḥ* on the nose; *oṃ hrīṃ kālāyai namaḥ* on the third line [of the face].
On the lips: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Kāmarūpiṇī; on the throat: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Raktyā; at the heart: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Kāmavardhanī; at the belly:

Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Pañcamukhinī; at the region of the navel: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Khaṭvāṅgahastā; in the right hand: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Ḍamarukahastā; in the left hand: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to [Ḍamarukahastā]. (Fifth line)

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Smṛti; at the vulva. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kāmavardhanī; on the right thigh. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kālakaṇṭhī; on the left thigh. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mahāmāyā; on the right knee. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Ūrdhvakeśinī;
on the left knee. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mohinī; on the right shank. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kālinī; on the [left shank]. (7th line)

On the left calf: *oṃ hrīṃ tārāyai namaḥ*; on the right foot: *oṃ hrīṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*; on the left foot: *oṃ hrīṃ grāmarakṣāyai namaḥ*. On the right breast: *oṃ hrīṃ niśīthinyai namaḥ*; on the left breast: *oṃ hrīṃ mālinyai namaḥ*. On the right side: *oṃ hrīṃ prabhāpuṣṭyai namaḥ*; on the left side.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) thus: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Daṃṣṭrākarāḷinī" at the top; "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalākṣiṇī" at the lower part;

and having uttered the pervasive power (*śakti*) extending to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), one should meditate upon [the deity] resembling a flash of lightning, appearing from the water within the hand, and having ascended the pitcher (*kumbha*): "Obeisance to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*)."

Having placed the *netra* [mantra] upon the eyes and filled the joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers, one should bring it down to one’s own station on the forehead— resembling ten million moons— with the mantra: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ bhadrakāḷicāmuṇḍi bhairavi rudhirādravā sarpavāsini hana hana śatrūn chindaya chindaya bhindaya bhindaya bhedaya bhedaya dāpaya dāpaya bimba śroṇi mama śiśuṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ śrīṃ binduśaktaye namaḥ |* (Placing the *netra* on the eyes, filling the *añjali* with flowers, and reciting the above, one brings the deity down to one’s own station on the forehead, which resembles ten million moons.)

Having meditated on the orb of the quarters whitened by funeral mounds, [the deity] emerges through the path of the flow of vital breath; having visualized [her] as being held within cupped hands, one should invoke her with the *mudrā* for summoning the object of focus.
One should meditate [on her] as four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with two feet; with hair standing erect, beautiful fangs, and possessed of a fierce gaze.
With her right leg extended and her left leg resting [on the ground], she holds a ḍamaru and a khaṭvāṅga in her right hands,
and a trident and a skull-cup in the space between her left hands.

The meditation on Cāmuṇḍā is described as follows: she is blue in color, possesses a magnificent form, laughs with a roar, has protruding lips, eyes like the *mātuḷuṅga* fruit, and is endowed with great wrath; she is fierce in appearance and wears a grand garb.

Having meditated thus, the wise one should worship the Great Goddess. Having performed the consecration of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), [he should recite] the great mantra of Bhadrakālī: *Oṃ hrīṃ mahācāmuṇḍīṃ*, *Oṃ hrīṃ vīracāmuṇḍīṃ*, *Oṃ haiṃ raktacāmuṇḍīṃ*.

Oṃ hoṃ khaṭgamūla ḍamarukakapāla hasti śrīṃ srīṃ klīṃ vara varada mahācāmuṇḍī svāhā. [Recite] the Cāmuṇḍā-gāyatrī three times: "We know the one who holds a sword in hand; we meditate upon the one who holds a trident in hand; may that Cāmuṇḍī inspire us."
Having invoked [the deity] with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], established her on the lotus seat with the *sthāpanī*,
made her present with the *sannidhānī*, and restrained her with the *niṣṭhurā*, one should offer the welcoming *arghya*;
O Goddess, sustainer of the entire world, [this continues] until the conclusion of the worship.
To that extent, by means of the state of self-identification,
your presence comes to be.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands, and having established oneness [with the deity] by means of the root mantra; having performed the protections (*rakṣā*), the veiling (*ava-kuṇṭhana*), and the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*); having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*); having displayed the *yonimudrā*; and having bathed [the deity] with drops from the *arghya* water after performing the anointing, rubbing with unguents, and immersion; [one offers] sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, mixed perfumes, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), flowers, *dūrvā* grass, a loin-cloth (*kaupīna*), a girdle (*mekhalā*), and a sacred thread (*upavīta*).
Having mentally offered with devotion earrings, armlets, garlands, and so forth, as well as variegated silk, cotton, and pure garments, and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers,

one should adorn [the deity] with Indra and the other [regents], ring the bell, and present incense, lamps, water for sipping, and the arghya offering; then, one should display the *manoratha-mudrā* and perform the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) at the points of dissolution.

Having prayed for the sake of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjārthaṃ*), [one should worship] in the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇe*) in the eight directions beginning with the east: *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnavināśanāya namaḥ*.

*Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ indrāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ māheśvaryai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ vārāhyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ bhadrakālyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ durgāyai namaḥ*.

"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadrā. Having thus worshipped, in the second enclosure, from the east to the northeast, [one should worship]: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Brāhmyāsana"; "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Brāhmī.
[One should meditate on her] as four-faced, large-eyed, and resembling molten collyrium.
She has four arms, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a rosary of beads.
She who has the form of a swan-bannered vehicle, who wears a crown of matted locks,
who sits upon a seat of red lotuses, and who is Brāhmī, the embodiment of all forms.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Brāhmī. Having worshipped her with all the ritual offerings beginning with invocation, [one recites]: "We meditate upon the one whose banner is the swan;
we contemplate the one whose hand holds the *kūrca*; may that Brāhmī inspire us."
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Māheśvarī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Māheśvarī.
She possesses a luster like a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and is joined with the dark-colored [Śiva].
She has three eyes, wears white garments, holds a trident in her hand, and has a bull as her emblem.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding a rosary,
wearing a crown of matted hair, the tranquil Maheśvarī, the consort of Śambhu.
Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hrīṃ māheśvaryai namaḥ*.
We know the one whose banner is the bull; we meditate upon the one who holds an axe in her hand; may that Māheśvarī inspire us.
*Oṃ hrīṃ kaumāryāsanāyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ Hrīṃ! Salutation to the form of Kaumāri,
who is joined with a cock, adorned with saffron breasts,
holding a spear and a javelin, and whose hands grant boons and fearlessness.
One should have the goddess, the daughter of the Mountain, fashioned as firmly mounted [on her vehicle], joined with [her consort], seated upon an eight-fold throne, and wearing garments of linen.
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kaumāri.
(Jya) We know the one whose banner is a cock; we meditate upon the one who holds a thunderbolt in his hand.
May that Kaumāri inspire us.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vaiṣṇavī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Vaiṣṇavī. [I worship] the Goddess who holds a conch and a discus, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness, who is endowed with a crown and diadem, and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
One should have the goddess Vaiṣṇavī fashioned— of dark complexion, with beautiful eyes,
seated upon a rājīvṛkṣa tree, endowed with the emblem of Garuḍa on her banner,
and adorned with all ornaments.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī. Let us meditate upon the one whose banner is Garuḍa; let us contemplate the one who holds the discus in his hand. May that Vaiṣṇavī inspire us.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Vārāhī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Vārāhī.
She is blue in color, of magnificent form, radiant with a crown of baskets, holding a black arrow, possessing fangs, and having a face like that of a boar.

One should mentally contemplate Vārāhī, who holds the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her hands, whose hand is joined with the moon, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
(6th line) *Oṃ hrīṃ vārāhyai namaḥ*. We know the one born from the buffalo; we meditate upon the one with the staff in her hand; may that Vārāhī inspire us.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Indrāṇī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Indrāṇī.
(Line 7) She has two eyes and four arms, is peaceful, and is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons;
she holds a thunderbolt and a spear, and possesses a complexion like gold and sapphire.
Indrāṇī, adorned with a crown of jewels, mounted upon an elephant.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Indrāṇī. (Jya) We know the one whose banner is an elephant; we meditate on the one who holds a thunderbolt in her hand. May that Indrāṇī inspire us.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the one seated upon Cāmuṇḍā. (9th line)
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Cāmuṇḍī— four-armed, with three eyes, having the color of a dark cloud,
her face formidable with protruding fangs, and clad in a tiger skin.
She wears bracelets and holds a trident; she bears a supreme skull-cup,
is adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, and is crowned with a jeweled casket.
I worship the one named Cāmuṇḍā, who is adorned with a garland of heads, seated upon a corpse as her vehicle, and endowed with all ornaments.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍī. (Jaya) We meditate upon her who is mounted upon a corpse; we contemplate her who holds a trident in her hand; may that Cāmuṇḍī inspire us.
(Third Line) Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the one seated on the throne of Śiva-Durgā; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva-Durgā.
Four-armed and two-eyed, dark-complexioned and in the full bloom of youth,
she holds a conch and a discus in her [lower] hands, while her upper hands display the gesture of granting fearlessness.
One should always meditate upon Śivadurgā, who is adorned with a crown and diadem, seated upon a buffalo, and endowed with all auspicious marks.

"May we know the one whose banner is the buffalo; may we meditate upon the one with long arms; may that Durgā inspire us. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in the third enclosure: Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kālikāli māṃsatoyāyai namaḥ || Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ raktakṛṣṇāyai svāhā || Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ haṃ haṃ kālikālarātri khaḍgadhāriṇī caṇḍī caṇḍacaṇḍīśakti ||

Śaṅkharī, Vallabhā, Dhyānaparā, Śakti, Śrīrūkteśvarī, Kuśamahākālī, Durgeśvarī, Oṃ (8th line), Kālī, Oṃ Pīṭhāhārī, Oṃ Namaśśivāya Svāhā. Oṃ Kālī Kālarātri Nīlaniṣṭhurī, [O you who] swallow all beings, Svāhā. Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Ākāśamāritī, Namaḥ.
(F.11b, 1st line)

Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ bhūtamāri, namas! Oṃ hrīṃ lokamāri, namas! Oṃ hrīṃ anantamāri, namas! Having thus worshipped [these] upon the pedestal, [one proceeds to] the fourth enclosure: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ divyayoginyai, namas! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ siddhayoginyai, namas! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ mahāyoginyai, namas! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ gaṇeśvaryai, namas! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ pretāśinyai, namas! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ ḍākinyai, namas!

(Third line) *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ kālinyai namaḥ | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ kālarātryai namaḥ | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ niśācaryai namaḥ | Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ ḍaṅkāriṇyai namaḥ*— having thus worshipped, (fourth line) in the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇe*): *Khaḍgāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Kapālāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Ghaṇṭāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Nārācāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Ḍamarukāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* (fifth line).
*Oṃ dhvajāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ vetālāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ kṣurikāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ pāśāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ vajrāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.

Having worshipped these with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the recitation of mantras (*japa*)—namely incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel leaf, and so forth—and having offered prayers, one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Following the path taught in the *Aśnikāya*, one should perform the rites up to the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in due order. In the midst of that, having invoked the Śakti, one should worship her along with her limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*). With sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*), one should offer one hundred oblations for each. The fuel-sticks should be of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *śamī*, *bilva*, *dūrvā*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *audumbara*. One should offer all of these with the root mantra, performing one hundred oblations for each. The *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, having given the *pūrṇāhuti*, having made an offering to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having presented incense and lamps, they should prepare the peace-pitchers (*śāntikumbha*) consecrated a hundred times with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and offered with the *sampātita* remains;

then they should proceed to the bathing pavilion. Thereafter, having raised the images from the midst of the water and having bid farewell to the world-protectors (*lokeśa*), [they should perform the bathing].
Having placed [the deity] upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), having consecrated him with the waters previously set out in the jars,

having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having paid obeisance; having mounted him onto the chariot and performed a circumambulation of the temple, one should bring him back to the bathing pavilion as before, place him upon the auspicious throne situated on the horse in the bathing area,
and perform the ritual of blocking the [senses’] forms (ākāra-rodhana).

Then, having bathed the image and other objects with clay, decoctions, cow’s urine, cow dung, ashes, perfumes, oil, wheat flour, powdered turmeric, myrobalan, and *bilva*, as well as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),

the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and various other waters; and having bathed them with milk and myrobalan water, with water containing gems, with jars filled from the Ocean of Milk, with water containing medicinal herbs, with thousands of streams of water from gold, gems, cows, horses, and the horns of bulls, and with water from conch shells and divine herbs—

Having bathed the image with water scented with *gandha* using the *Gaṅgātīrtha* [mantra], and having consecrated the stone with the *Śaktimūla* [mantra] and the *Ādhāraśakti* mantra, one should adorn it with ointments, ornaments, flower garlands, and so forth;

having worshipped it fully, offered the *ācamana* and *arghya* with the *Hṛdaya* [mantra], and presented incense, lamps, *nīrājana*, collyrium, and the rest, one should apply the protective *tilaka* that wards off demons and bind the *pratisara* thread. Then, upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared on the altar, [one should perform the rite] with the *Hṛdaya* [mantra].

Having spread out *kuśa* grass and formed the *svastika* diagram, one should place a skull-topped staff (*khaḍvāṅga*) upon it; then, layering above that skins, hair, shorn hair, and armor, and having spread out a bed with its pillows and all its furnishings, one should place the sleep-vessel (*nidrākumbha*) in due order upon those on the couch. Having worshipped the deities beginning with Brāhmī in the directions starting from the east, one should worship the guardians of the world (*lokapāla*) together with their vehicles and weapons in the eight directions beginning from the east for the protection of the image.

Having meditated upon and worshipped [the deity], and having offered the food offering (naivedya), incense, and lamps, one should thus assign the thirty-one principles of the intermediate space (antarikṣa) along with their presiding deities: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva.
(5th line) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Indrā, the presiding deity of the Śiva-tattva. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jñānī, the presiding deity of the Vidyā-tattva.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kriyā, the sovereign of the principle of the self. (6th line) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of illusion (*māyātattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gahaneśa, the sovereign of the principle of illusion. On the right side: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of time (*kālatattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ekālanāman, the sovereign of the principle of time. (7th line)

On the left side: *Oṃ hrīṃ kalā-tattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ kalā-tattvādhipāyai jñāna-bindave namaḥ*. In the heart: *Oṃ hrīṃ niyati-tattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ niyati-tattvādhipāyai niyāmakāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ vidyā-tattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ vidyā-tattvādhipāyai vedavijñānāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ rāga-tattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ rāga-tattvādhipāyai kāmadāya namaḥ*. In the belly: *Oṃ hrīṃ prakṛti-tattvāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ Hrīṃ! Salutation to Pradhānakāya, the presiding deity of the principle of Prakṛti (oṃ hrīṃ prakṛtitattvādhipāyai pradhānakāya namaḥ).

On the back [of the image], oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to the principle of Guṇa (oṃ hrīṃ guṇatattvāya namaḥ). Between the navel and the private parts, oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to Trideha, the presiding deity of the principle of Guṇa (oṃ hrīṃ guṇatattvādhipāyai tridehāya namaḥ). Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to the principle of Buddhi (oṃ hrīṃ buddhitattvāya namaḥ). Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to Buddhi, the presiding deity of the principle of Buddhi (oṃ hrīṃ buddhitattvādhipāyai buddhyai namaḥ). At the three joints, oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to the principle of Ahaṃkāra (oṃ hrīṃ ahaṃkāratattvāya namaḥ). Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutation to Haṃkṛti, the presiding deity of the principle of Ahaṃkāra (oṃ hrīṃ ahaṃkāratattvādhipāyai haṃkṛte namaḥ).

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of mind (*manastattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the intention (*saṅkalpa*), the presiding deity of the principle of mind. (Third line) In the ear: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of hearing (*śrotratattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vyomacāriṇī, the presiding deity of the principle of hearing. In the skin: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of touch (*tvaktattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarvāṅgā, the presiding deity of the principle of touch. (Fourth line) In the eye: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of sight (*cakṣustattva*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Prakāśakā, the presiding deity of the principle of sight. In the tongue: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the tongue (*jihvātattva*). (Fifth line)

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Great Vajra, the lord of the principle of the tongue. At the nose: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the nose. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vilambaka, the lord of the principle of the nose.

At the mouth: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of speech. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dundubhi, the lord of the principle of speech. (6th line) At the hands: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the hand. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sāmadā, the lord of the principle of the hand. At the feet: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the principle of the foot. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ramaṇa, the lord of the principle of the foot. (7th line)

At the anus: *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the principle of the anus (*pāyu-tattva*); *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the sovereign of the principle of the anus, Turṇakṛt. At the generative organ (*upastha*): *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the principle of the generative organ (*upastha-tattva*); *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the sovereign of the principle of the generative organ, Ghanāndā. At the navel: *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the principle of sound (*śabda-tattva*); *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the sovereign of the principle of sound, Sūkṣmanāda.
At the head: *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*); *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the sovereign of the principle of touch, Balavaktra. At the forehead: [continue as above].

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of form (rūpa-tattva). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Bhānumatī, the presiding deity of the principle of form. At the mouth: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of taste (rasa-tattva). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Jaladā, the presiding deity of the principle of taste.

At the heart: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of smell (gandha-tattva). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gandhāṅga, the presiding deity of the principle of smell. (Third line) At the navel: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of space (vyoma-tattva). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vyomacārī, the presiding deity of the principle of space. At the yoni: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the principle of air (vāyu-tattva). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to [the presiding deity] of the principle of air. (Fourth line)

Homage to Mātariśvan. At the secret place: Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to the fire principle (agnitattva). Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to Tviṣāṃnidhi, the presiding deity of the fire principle. Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to the water principle (aptattva). Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to Jaleśa, the presiding deity of the water principle. (Fifth line) At the feet: Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to the earth principle (pṛthvītattva). Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to Śrīkaṇṭha, the presiding deity of the earth principle. At the position of the knees, having offered a flower garland and a protective thread for the sake of unimpeded vision. (Sixth line)

Above the *kuṇḍa*: *Oṃ hrīṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ śivatattvādhipāyai icchāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ vidyātattvādhipāyai jñānyai namaḥ*. (7th line) Below the knees: *Oṃ hrīm ātmatattvāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrī ātmatattvādhipāyai kriyāyai namaḥ*. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should worship each portion in sequence from the east to the end of the directions: *Oṃ hāṃ dhūṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ dhūṃ kṣmāmūrtyādhīpāyai ūrdhvakeśinyai namaḥ*. (F.14a, 1st line)
Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Vanhimūrti (the Fire-form).

Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Virūpākṣī, the presiding deity of Vanhimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, obeisance to Yajamānamūrti (the Sacrificer-form). Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, obeisance to Śuṣkāṅgī, the presiding deity of Yajamūrti.
Oṃ hāṃ ṣūṃ, obeisance to Makārka-mūrti.
Oṃ hāṃ ṣūmakārka, obeisance to the mistress of the earth-form (*mūrti*), Narabhojinī. Oṃ hāṃ vyūṃ, obeisance to the water-form (*jalamūrti*).
Oṃ hāṃ vyūṃ, obeisance to the mistress of the water-form, Pharśakā. Oṃ hāṃ yuṃ, obeisance to the wind-form (*vāyumūrti*).
Oṃ yuṃ, obeisance to the mistress of the wind-form, Dhūmrākṣiṇī. (Fourth Line)

Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the desired form (*iṣṭamūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, obeisance to the sovereign of the desired form, the one of universal form (*viśvarūpiṇī*). Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ khaṃ, obeisance to the form of space (*khamūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ khaṃ, obeisance to the sovereign of the form of space, the terrifier (*bhayaṃkṛtī*).

(5th line) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Having thus invoked and worshipped [them], and having propitiated the Lords of the World (*lokeśas*) in their midst, one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and [worship] the four digits (*kalās*), beginning with Nivṛtti, upon the girdles (*mekhalās*) in the middle of the pit. (6th line)
Having placed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) at the navel and the bliss (*ānanda*) of the lips,

and having performed the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) together with the deities of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila-vahni*) and the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*), one should offer three oblations according to the sequence of joining. Then, from the mouth of the Preceptor,

having worshipped the Mistress of each Principle (*tattveśvarī*) and the Form and its Lord (*mūrti-mūrtīśvara*) in their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer three oblations with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and other materials.

One should offer oblations until each [deity] is satisfied with one hundred and eight counts, or otherwise, one should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth of the total number of oblations performed for the Guru.

Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti" and offered three oblations, one should worship the Ātmatattva and its presiding deity, offering three oblations to each; then, having worshipped the Mūrti and the Mūrtīśvarī, one should offer three oblations to each.

For the sake of purifying the Brahma-portion, one should offer oblations with the root-mantra and the limbs (*aṅga*) of Brahmā, each accompanied by a full hundred. The image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*) should also offer oblations to the Guru, using a tenth part of the total oblations. Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), they should pour the remnants into the Peace-pitchers (*śāntikumbha*). Holding the Peace-pitchers, which have been consecrated by the pouring of those remnants, they should go into the presence of the Goddess. Standing in their respective directions, they should sprinkle the Brahma-portion with the water from the Peace-pitchers using the roots of *kuśa* grass.

Having touched [the vessel], they should perform recitations equal in number to the oblations. The Guru, having brought about the presence of their heart-deities, performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and concealed [them] with the *avakuṇṭhana* rite, should restrain them and cause the presiding principle (*tattvādhipa*) to hear [this]:
"O Goddess, as long as there are defects arising here, you must remain right here through your presence. They should then sprinkle [the area] with water from the pitcher using fallen leaves.

Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ! Salutation to the two presiding deities of the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, who are the embodiments of Kriyā and Jñāna. Oṃ oṃ lūṃ lūṃ! Salutation to the two embodiments of Lakṣmī and Mūrti. Oṃ oṃ hṛdā hṛdaṃ! Salutation to the two embodiments of Fire and Hṛdaya.
Salutation to the two Virūpākṣas. Oṃ oṃ śraṃ śraṃ! Salutation to the two presiding deities of the Sacrificer and Mūrti.
Oṃ oṃ śūṃ śūmakārkamūrtibhyāṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ oṃ śūṃ śūmakārkamūrtyādhipābhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ oṃ vayūṃ vyūṃ jalamūrtibhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ oṃ vyūṃ vyūṃ jalamūrtyadhipābhyāṃ pharśakārībhyāṃ namaḥ. Oṃ oṃ yūṃ yūṃ vāyumūrtibhyāṃ namaḥ.

Oṃ oṃ yūṃ yūṃ, salutations to the two Dhūmrākṣīs, the presiding deities of the Vāyu-mūrti; oṃ oṃ sūṃ sūṃ, salutations to the two Viśvarūpiṇīs, the presiding deities of the Miṣṭa-mūrti; oṃ oṃ huṃ huṃ, salutations to the two Khaṃ-mūrtis;

oṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, salutations to the two Bhayaṅkārīs, the presiding deities of the Khaṃ-mūrti—having worshipped thus, one should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and perform the libation as before.

Having gratified and worshipped each image and its presiding deity (mūrtīśvarī), they should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* as before. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and performed the *sampātābhihavana* (pouring the remnants of the oblation) into the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*), they should take it and go near the Goddess.

As before, preceded by sprinkling with the water of peace (*śāntyaṃbhas*), they should touch the middle part [of the vessel] with the middle blade of *kuśa* grass while reciting the root mantra. Having performed the recitation equal in number to the oblations and having sprinkled it again with the water of peace, they should perform the *sannidhi*, *avaguṇṭhana*, and *nirodhana* rites using the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having issued the command to the ignorant one, he should cause [the mantra] to be heard: "O Lord of the Vidya-tattva, as long as the image is raised up by the defects of the ignorant, so long must you remain right here through your presence. *Oṃ hīṃ huṃ vidyā-tattva...

śiva-tattvābhyāṃ namaḥ.* *Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ vidyā-tattva śiva-tattvābhyāṃ jñānī-icchābhyāṃ namaḥ.* Having worshipped the Mūrtīśvarī in each form according to the previous method of conjunction (*sandhāna-krama*), [he proceeds] to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having proceeded according to the sequence of reintegration (*saṃdhāna*), and having worshipped for the sake of reintegration, one should satisfy [the deities] individually with three oblations each. Then, having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) along with its presiding goddesses, the *icchā-śakti*, and the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), and having worshipped and satisfied them, one should worship the Form (*mūrti*) and the Mistress of the Form (*mūrtīśvarī*). Having offered incense as before, they should perform the *saṃhitā*-oblations as previously described.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having performed the rites as before, he should take the *śāntikumbha* (peace-pitcher), go to the presence of the Goddess, and sprinkle [the area] with the waters from the *śāntikumbha*. Touching the portion of the enemy with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) the number of times prescribed for the *homa*, and sprinkling again with the water of peace, he should perform the *sannidhi* (invocation of presence), *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling), and *nirodhana* (confinement) with the *hṛdaya-mantra* as before. Then he should proclaim his desire and obtain permission, saying: "O Sovereign of the Śiva-tattva, may there be no fault through my transgressions."

"O Goddess Śuddhitā, you must remain right here by virtue of your presence. Having thus informed [the deity] and performed everything upon the seat, he invokes her with "oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti," worships her with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), performs the *pūrṇāhuti*, offers water for sipping (*ācamana*), and presents betel-leaf and other items. Having confined the Goddess, offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, presented the inner and outer *bali* offerings, and dismissed the *bali* mantras, he cleanses his ears and mouth, approaches the Goddess, worships her with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and [addresses] the Blessed Lady in three parts.

Having informed the Blessed One through knowledge that [the ritual] has proceeded from karma due to delusion—even regarding the three portions beginning with Brahmā—[one should say]: "Let whatever karma is full or incomplete be fulfilled by one's own power and accepted. Having thus made this request, [one should offer] the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *anutmantra* and the body [of the deity]. "Obeisance to the gracious Vighneśvara. This is the procedure for the consecration (*adhivāsana*). Then, on the second day at dawn, having performed the two daily rites (*nityāhnika*), together with the *mūrtipas*...

Having gone to the Makhālaya, having removed the *nirmālya*, and having performed the ritual beginning with the worship of the Sun (*sūryapūjā*) and ending with the libation of mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*) as before, one should enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). Having performed the placement of the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*) and the gems (*ratnanyāsa*) and so forth as before, and having installed the Goddess as before, one should perform the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*). Then, by means of the mantras of the seat (*āsana*), the form (*mūrti*), and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), as well as the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), one should perform the placement of the *Tattveśvarī* and the *Gaurī-kalā*. Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should take up the water-pots (*kumbha*) at an auspicious moment and proceed in a clockwise direction.

Having led [the deity] into the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and having installed it in due order upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front, one should take the seed-syllable (bīja) from the *vardhanī* vessel and, having invoked the deity with the root mantra, sprinkle the head with water from the *kumbha*.

Having sprinkled [the deity] in sequence starting from the east with the eightfold handfuls of water (*aṣṭaśaktikaraka*), and having offered incense and lamps, performed the ritual waving of lights (*nīrāñjana*), applied sacred ash and sandalwood paste, and conferred blessings (*āśirvāda*), one should thereafter perform the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) and present the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) endowed with the six flavors.

Having offered coconuts, plantains, jackfruits, and other fruits as well as betel leaves, and having performed the worship of the Brahmins preceded by the worship of the Ācārya and the Sādhaka; and having performed the ten gifts (*daśadāna*), the gift for the procession (*yātrādāna*), and the gift of the drum (*bheridāna*) according to the procedure prescribed in the *Yāmalāgama*;
[he should offer] the sixteen types of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), flour-cakes, lamps, five plantain leaves, coconuts and other fruits, as well as a lion, an elephant, and a horse.

Having slain cows, buffaloes, goats, chickens, pigs, peacocks, tigers, and other wild animals, the deities feel ashamed; therefore, accompanied by all musical instruments and the sound of *arghya* offerings, one should perform circumambulation of the village and other sites starting from the east, and offer the *bali* oblation in the cardinal and intermediate directions. One should enter with all musical instruments during the appropriate time.

[Thus ends the ritual procedure for the installation of Bhadrakālī in the Yamalāgama. Salutations to the illustrious Kālabhairava. Salutations to Kriyā; salutations to Jñānī; salutations to Icchā; salutations to Kuṭilāśakti. In the first enclosure: salutations to Sarvavighnavināśinī; second, salutations to Māheśvarī.

Salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; salutation to Vārāhī; salutation to Cāmuṇḍā; salutation to Bhadrakālī; salutation to Durgā; salutation to Vīrabhadra. (Part-c) In the third enclosure: salutation to Brāhmī; salutation to Suśivadurgā. (Part-d) In the fourth enclosure: salutation to Divyayoginī; salutation to Siddhayoginī; salutation to Mahāyoginī; salutation to Gaṇeśvarī; salutation to Pretanāśinī.

(Part-e) Homage to Ḍākinī! Homage to Kālinī! Homage to Kālarātri! Homage to Niśācarī! Homage to Ḍhakkāriṇī! In the fifth enclosure: (Part-f) To the sword, *huṃ phaṭ*! Homage to the skull-cup, to the bell, to the iron arrow, to the hand-drum, to the banner, to the razor, to the noose, to the vajra! *Oṃ hrīṃ mahācāmuṇḍīṃ*, *oṃ hrīṃ vīracāmuṇḍīṃ* (...), *oṃ haiṃ raktacāmuṇḍīṃ*, *oṃ hoṃ khaḍga śūla* (...).

*Ḍamuraka kapāla hastīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ vara vara mahābhadrakālyai svāhā*. [One should meditate on] her who is beautiful, with dark hair like the moon, having the form of a blue lotus petal, with a very well-proportioned and lovely face, adorned with all ornaments, holding a conch and a discus, granting fearlessness with her right hand, and possessing a magnificent form with her left hand.

One should meditate upon Durgā—the slayer of the Daityas, well-composed with breasts bound together, stationed upon the head of Mahiṣa, endowed with the color of a mango—and having visualized her, one should invoke her. (Part-c) [He should visualize] Andhaka, who has a single face and a flaming head, eight red eyes, is clad in blue garments, and likewise possesses terrible teeth;
he stands upon the head of Mahiṣa, holding his right foot, while [Durgā] holds his left tooth at the waist of Mahiṣa, and the tip of her trident rises from the chest of Mahiṣa. (F.19b, first line)
(…) And indeed, [the syllable] *gu* with two *bha*s, [the syllable] *kha* with a *bhasta*, and in the mouth another *kapāla* and a sword (*khaḍga*).
(3rd line) (…) [The syllable] *ye* (…) joined with *hasa*, [and] *gamaśca kṛ*. (4th line)
(…) All songs are adorned; likewise, O Left One, you are on the right path of the two-footed one.
(5th line) … I consider you difficult to attain … | (F.20a 1st line)
Dark-complexioned, clad in red garments, and endowed with flaming veins, they emerge from the eight lingas;
[the first] holds a skull-cup and a sword, while in his left hand he carries a *ḍamaru* drum, and below that, another bell.

Obeisance to you, Bhadrakālī, who holds a pestle, whose nature is that of Rudra, who possesses three eyes, whose face is [radiant], and who is the peak of the world of manifestation. O Mother, obeisance to you!
